content: Trichotillomania (TTM), also known as hair-pulling disorder, is a common and debilitating condition characterized by repetitive hair-pulling behavior. This review evaluates the effects of various medications for TTM in adults, children, and adolescents, comparing them to placebo or other medications. 1. Antioxidants in Adults: A single trial using silymarin showed little to no difference in treatment response between the antioxidant group (35.7%) and the placebo group (28.6%) after six weeks. The risk ratio (RR) was 2.25 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84 to 5.99), based on low-certainty evidence. No dropouts were reported in either group. 2. Antioxidants in Adolescents: A single trial using silymarin in adolescents also showed little to no difference in treatment response between the antioxidant group (50%) and the placebo group (25%) after six weeks. The RR was 2.00 (95% CI 0.28 to 14.20), based on low-certainty evidence. No dropouts were reported in either group. 3. Antipsychotics in Adults: A single trial using olanzapine suggested a potentially greater treatment response in the antipsychotic group (85%) compared to the placebo group (17%) after 12 weeks. The RR was 5.08 (95% CI 1.4 to 18.37), based on low-certainty evidence. No dropouts were reported in either group. 4. Cell Signal Transducers in Adults: A single trial using inositol showed little to no difference in treatment response between the cell signal transducer group (42.1%) and the placebo group (31.6%) after 10 weeks. The RR was 1.33 (95% CI 0.57 to 3.11), based on low-certainty evidence. No dropouts were reported in either group. 5. Glutamate Modulators in Adults: A single trial using N-acetylcysteine indicated a probable greater treatment response in the glutamate modulator group (56%) compared to the placebo group (16%) after 12 weeks. The RR was 3.5 (95% CI 1.34 to 9.17), based on moderate-certainty evidence. No dropouts were reported in either group. 6. Glutamate Modulators in Children and Adolescents: A single trial using N-acetylcysteine in children and adolescents showed little to no difference in treatment response between the glutamate modulator group (25%) and the placebo group (21.1%). The RR was 1.19 (95% CI 0.37 to 3.77), based on low-certainty evidence. Dropouts due to adverse events were also similar between the groups (5% in the glutamate modulator group vs. 0% in the placebo group; RR 2.86, 95% CI 0.12 to 66.11). 7. Opioid Antagonists in Adults: Two studies using naltrexone suggested there may be little to no difference in treatment response between the opioid antagonist group (37.5%) and the placebo group (25%) after six to eight weeks. The RR was 2.14 (95% CI 0.25 to 18.17), based on very low-certainty evidence. No data were available regarding dropouts due to adverse events. 8. Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) in Adults: No data were available for treatment response to SSRIs. However, two trials using fluoxetine showed little to no difference in dropouts due to adverse events between the SSRI group (5.1%) and the placebo group (0%) after 6 to 12 weeks. The RR was 3.00 (95% CI 0.33 to 27.62), based on low-certainty evidence. 9. Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs) with Predominantly Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SRI) Actions in Adults: A single trial using clomipramine suggested a potentially greater treatment response in the TCA group (40%) compared to the placebo group (0%) after nine weeks. The RR was 5.73 (95% CI 0.36 to 90.83), based on very low-certainty evidence. There may also be increased dropouts due to adverse events in the TCA group (30%) compared to the placebo group (0%), with an RR of 4.45 (95% CI 0.27 to 73.81). 10. TCAs with Predominantly SRI Actions versus Other TCAs in Adults: A single trial comparing clomipramine to desipramine suggested a potentially greater treatment response in the clomipramine group after five weeks. The mean difference (MD) was -4.00 (95% CI -6.13 to -1.87), based on low-certainty evidence. No dropouts were reported in either group. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to definitively confirm or refute the efficacy of any specific medication or class of medications for the treatment of TTM in adults, children, or adolescents. Preliminary findings suggest that N-acetylcysteine, clomipramine, and olanzapine may have beneficial effects in adults, but these results are based on small sample sizes and require further investigation.
